question: How to improve site safety when using robotics?

answer.answer:
**Summary**

Only one cited path leads to improved site safety (VA13), and it is not a machine: moving work off site through prefabrication (PR2), which is backed by peer-reviewed evidence and carried by 12 of the 50 coded cases. On site, the lever the standards support is collaborative working (human-robot interaction, CO6), which mitigates work safety concern (RI20) under power-and-force limits, but it comes with two upstream requirements that must be met first, workforce training (RI6) and regulatory/legal compliance (RI18), and the training one is by far the heavier, carried by 27 of the 50 against 2. Two things practitioners actually use for safety, remote-control (CO8) at 18 of the 50 and reduce disruption due to hazards (VA25) at 13, have no cited dependency at all, so if you rely on them you are ahead of the literature, not behind it.

**The one cited route into site safety**

Improve site safety (VA13) is a Value, drawn on by 39 of the 50 coded cases, and it carries exactly one dependency edge in the whole graph, an inbound one: prefabrication/off-site (PR2) enablesCapability improve site safety (VA13), peer-reviewed, carried by 12 of the 50 coded cases, on the reasoning that moving work offsite improves site safety [1]. That is the complete edge set for VA13, so the statement that only one cited path reaches it is exact and quotable, not an artefact of retrieval. VA13 is recorded as applying in the Structural Construction phase, in a value-realizing role. [2]

If you take that route, PR2 itself is drawn on by 20 of the 50 coded cases [1] and brings its own upstream requirements, which are organisational rather than technical:

- DfMA for DFAB process (PR9) enablesCapability prefabrication/off-site (PR2), peer-reviewed, carried by 15 of the 50 [1];
- early contractor involvement (CO11) enablesCapability PR2, carried by 13 of the 50, on the basis that integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase [1];
- integrate supply chain (VA14) enablesCapability PR2, carried by 12 of the 50 [1];
- PR2 dependsOn rely on precise planning (RI14), carried by 18 of the 50: prefabrication relies on precise up-front planning and logistics [1], with RI14 drawn on by 36 of the 50 [1];
- PR2 dependsOn regulatory/legal concern (RI18), carried by 10 of the 50, where a functional regulatory system for offsite compliance requires third-party certification and traceability [1].

None of these five is a Resource. The safety gain routed through PR2 is bought with design method, procurement timing, supply-chain integration and planning discipline, not with equipment.

**On-site safety: collaboration, training and the standards**

Where work stays on site, the cited mechanism runs through human-robot interaction (CO6), a Condition drawn on by 32 of the 50 coded cases [1]. Its three edges are all outbound and all listed, so they can be quoted as complete:

- CO6 mitigates work safety concern (RI20), evidence grade standard, carried by 4 of the 50, on the mechanism that power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigates contact-injury risk [1];
- CO6 dependsOn require workforce training (RI6), peer-reviewed, carried by 27 of the 50: the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [1];
- CO6 dependsOn regulatory/legal concern (RI18), evidence grade standard, carried by 2 of the 50, namely compliance with the robot safety standards [1].

Read the relations rather than the arrows: in both dependsOn edges, RI6 and RI18 are the requirements and sit upstream of CO6 in practice, while CO6 sits upstream of the risk it mitigates. The asymmetry between the two requirements is the finding here. Workforce training is carried by 27 of the 50 on CO6's edge and RI6 is drawn on by 44 of the 50 coded cases [1]; the standards-compliance edge is carried by 2, with RI18 drawn on by 12 of the 50 [1]. Training is what the record actually shows being done. On RI20 itself, only CO6's edge is in front of me out of three cited edges in total, with RI20 drawn on by 13 of the 50 [1], so I cannot tell you what else reaches it.

**The deployed record**

Three deployed processes in this context were adopted expressly to address safety, and all three do on-site work rather than factory work: census_RXM23-1 performs drilling on the structural core and sitework, at technology readiness level 7 [3]; census_RXM4-5 performs digging and material handling on sitework, substructure and foundation, at technology readiness level 8 [4]; and census_RXM1-3 performs digging and material handling on sitework, at technology readiness level 8 [5]. The context gives no firm behind any of the three, and it does not link them to particular enablers, so I cannot say which of the enablers above they exhibit. What they do show is a gap worth noting: the safety-motivated deployments in front of me remove the worker from hazardous on-site tasks directly, whereas the only cited path to VA13 removes the work itself to a factory.

**Widely used, not yet connected**

Several enablers that bear directly on site safety carry no cited dependency edge at all, which is a property of the literature rather than of the record: the cited layer has 100 edges touching 68 of the 140 enablers, leaving 72 with none, and an edge-free enabler is present and usable, evidenced by how many of the 50 cases draw on it [1]. Remote-control (CO8, a Condition) is drawn on by 18 of the 50 and carries no dependency edges [1]; reduce disruption due to hazards (VA25, a Value) by 13 of the 50, also with no edges [1]. Most striking, significant human involvement (RE6) is drawn on by all 50 coded cases and has no edge [1], and it co-occurs with improve site safety in 39 cases [1], a correlation and not a dependency. Robotics on a Japanese site is not an unmanned condition, and any safety case has to be written around people being present.

**Two practical constraints**

If the robot moves, site conditions bite the planning layer: location dependent/site constraint (RI5) constrains path-planning (PR12), peer-reviewed, carried by 15 of the 50, because reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors and localisation method choice is constrained [1]. RI5 is drawn on by 21 of the 50 [1] and PR12 by 26 of the 50 [1]. And the Mobile attribute (AT9) enablesCapability on-site DFAB (PR8), carried by 9 of the 50, through a mobile robot with autonomous repositioning and localisation [1], with AT9 drawn on by 28 of the 50 [1]. Neither edge terminates at VA13, so treat them as operating conditions for safe on-site work, not as cited safety benefits.

A note on scope: retrieval read "robotics" broadly, taking in robotic assembly (PR4), robotic drilling (PR19), gantry-type robotic system (RE10) and unmanned mobile vehicle (RE15) as well as the robotic arm (RE2). That widening does not change the answer, because none of those enablers has a cited edge to VA13; robotic pickup/selection (PR15) co-occurs with improve site safety at weight 18 [6] and human-robot interaction co-occurs with it at weight 28 [7], but those are statistical correlations across cases, not directional dependencies.
